title: Profit and Loss and Discount: The Mathematics of Buying and Selling

questions.question: An article sold for 540 rupees gives a profit of 20 percent. Its cost price is:
questions.rationale: SP = CP x 1.2, so CP = 540/1.2 = 450 rupees. Dividing out the profit factor recovers the base — always divide, never subtract 20 percent of 540.

questions.question: Two articles are sold at the same price, one at 20 percent profit and the other at 20 percent loss. The overall result is:
questions.rationale: Same-SP equal profit-and-loss percentages always net a loss of (P/10)^2 = (20/10)^2 = 4 percent. The loss item drags the total below zero because its cost price is larger.

questions.question: Successive discounts of 20 percent and 10 percent equal a single discount of:
questions.rationale: Combined = a + b - ab/100 = 20 + 10 - 200/100 = 28 percent. Check with 100: 100 -> 80 -> 72, a single cut of 28.

questions.question: A trader marks his goods 40 percent above cost price and allows a 25 percent discount on the marked price. His profit percent is:
questions.rationale: SP = 1.40 x 0.75 x CP = 1.05 CP — a 5 percent profit. Multiply the factors: 1.4 x 0.75 = 1.05.

questions.question: A shopkeeper claims to sell at cost price but uses a 900 g weight in place of 1 kg. His gain percent is:
questions.rationale: Gain = error/(true - error) x 100 = 100/900 x 100 = 11.11 percent. He pockets the value of 100 g on every 900 g actually delivered.

questions.question: The cost price of 15 articles equals the selling price of 12 articles. The profit percent is:
questions.rationale: Take the common value as 60: CP = 4 per article, SP = 5 per article, profit = (5-4)/4 = 25 percent. Generally m/n pairs give (m-n)/n profit.

questions.question: A shopkeeper marks a shirt at 1500 rupees, allows a 20 percent discount, and still makes a 20 percent profit. The cost price is:
questions.rationale: SP = 1500 x 0.80 = 1200. CP = 1200/1.2 = 1000. Two multiplications walk the chain MP -> SP -> CP.

questions.question: A man sells an article at 10 percent loss. To recover the loss, at what profit percent must he sell a second identical article?
questions.rationale: Recovery percent = x/(10 - x) x 100 for a loss of x = 10: 10/90 x 100 = 11.11 percent. Selling the second at 10 percent profit only breaks even on a DIFFERENT base — the classic trap.

questions.question: By selling 45 mangoes at the price of 50 bought mangoes, a fruit-seller's profit or loss percent is:
questions.rationale: CP of 50 = SP of 45. Take common value 450: CP = 9, SP = 10 per mango — profit (10-9)/9 = 11.11 percent. Same false-weight logic, now friendly.

questions.question: A price is first marked up 25 percent and then discounted 25 percent (both on the then-current price). The net effect is:
questions.rationale: 1.25 x 0.75 = 0.9375, a 6.25 percent loss. Equal markup-then-markdown on moving bases always lands below the start — the (x/10)^2 family again with x = 25.
